agent_scope: Evidence pack for the four HeroEngine (Idea Fabrik / Laniatus) engine_tools codes h_blade, h_cloud, h_hsl and h_instancing, covering documented capability, vendor-stated numbers, known limits and confirmed game usage, with explicit gaps where evidence is absent.

sources.applicability_note: Live vendor landing/login page only. Confirms the product still had a hosted web presence and names the current rights-holders and a 'Version: 3.0' label. It contains no technical, architectural or pricing detail and does not prove the engine is actively developed.

sources.title: Idea Fabrik PLC (official corporate site)

claims.statement: HeroBlade is the vendor's single integrated client/toolset for HeroEngine: world building, particle effects, lighting, audio, animation wiring, game mechanics and core systems are all authored inside the HeroBlade client, and nearly any object, particle, emitter, character or asset property can be edited from its Properties Sheet Panel.
claims.locator: Section 'All-in-one Development Environment' (heading and first paragraph)
claims.context: Vendor marketing description of HeroBlade circa 2013 (archived page). Establishes intended scope, not measured capability.

claims.statement: HeroBlade is built for simultaneous multi-user editing: teams in different geographic locations work on nearly any aspect of the same live world at once, and the vendor states project management and whiteboarding are linked directly to the 3D environment and to game scripts.
claims.locator: Sections 'Massively Collaborative' (bullet 'Integrated project management and whiteboarding linked to 3D environment and game scripts') and 'Project Management Tools'
claims.context: Vendor description of the collaborative model. It does not state how many editors can work concurrently or what synchronisation latency is achieved.

claims.statement: The world-building workflow inside HeroBlade is real-time and collaborative: multiple teams can build and dress an area from any location, and QA teams review new areas and annotate issues in 3D space, after which changes are assigned to a team or individual.
claims.locator: Section 'Real-time Collaborative World Building'
claims.context: Vendor world-building page (archived). Confirms intended QA/annotation workflow; no throughput or latency figures are given.

claims.statement: HeroEngine supports up to 256 textures in each of up to 4 texture layers; every texture channel can carry a bump and specularity map with its own mapping, UV scaling, bump and specularity strength, and any heightmap vertex can be tinted by painting colour on it.
claims.locator: Section 'Texture Layers', sentence 'HeroEngine has a tremendous freedom of textures with support for up to 256 textures in each of the up to 4 layers'
claims.context: Vendor world-building page (archived). This is a stated design maximum for the 2013-era engine, not a measured rendering limit.

claims.statement: No source opened in this assignment quantifies HeroBlade editor performance - neither the maximum number of concurrent collaborating editors, nor world-sync latency, nor the practical size of an editable area. All opened sources describe HeroBlade capabilities qualitatively.
claims.locator: HEWIKI Main Page: 'World Building' and 'Project Management Tools' section listings contain no performance page; the feature pages opened (SRC-HE-006/007) give no figures
claims.context: Gap, not a compatibility claim. Missing evidence would be an official HeroBlade performance document or a measured multi-editor benchmark.

game_examples.fact: Announced in 2008 as being built with Simutronics' HeroEngine, and the shipped title's engine field is HeroEngine; the studio later confirmed the game 'was originally created in HeroEngine'.
game_examples.locator: SRC-HE-003 body paragraph 'is being built with Simutronics' HeroEngine development platform'; SRC-HE-015 section 'Next Steps'
game_examples.non_transferable: Proves the title shipped on the HeroEngine platform, whose editor is HeroBlade. It does NOT prove which individual HeroBlade tools were used, nor that the shipped client still contains HeroBlade code (the studio states little original code remains).

game_examples.fact: A short-lived (May-August 2011) free-to-play MMORPG whose infobox engine field is HeroEngine; the HeroEngine encyclopedia article separately notes its roughly 18-month development cycle.
game_examples.locator: SRC-HE-017 infobox 'Engine: HeroEngine' and sentence 'It makes use of the engine HeroEngine'; SRC-HE-002 section 'Features' ('Faxion Online took 18 months to complete')
game_examples.non_transferable: Evidences that a second, independent studio shipped a HeroEngine title. It does NOT evidence HeroCloud hosting or any specific HeroBlade tool, and the engine attribution rests on a secondary mirror.

claims.statement: HeroCloud was the vendor's cloud-hosted license: 'ONLY $99 a year' bought a license to the HeroEngine plus cloud hosting of the development and live servers, with the vendor retaining 30% of revenue once the game was published.
claims.locator: Section 'HeroCloud: HeroEngine in the Cloud, ONLY $99 a year' (price) and paragraph 'Once (or if) your game is published and begins making money, we keep 30% of revenue'
claims.context: 2013 vendor list price and revenue-share term (archived page). Both figures appear verbatim in the vendor's own licensing page and are corroborated by SRC-HE-005/013 and SRC-HE-004.

claims.statement: The alternative HeroEngine source-code license was listed at a base price of $75,000 with a 7% revenue share.
claims.locator: Section 'HeroEngine Source Code': 'The basic HeroEngine source code license is $75,000 with a 7% revenue share'
claims.context: 2013 vendor list price (archived page). 'Various licensing models available depending on your financial needs', so this is the stated basic tier only.

claims.statement: HeroCloud was positioned as a managed platform-as-a-service: the vendor hosted the server in the cloud for free during development and after launch, supplied integrated billing, and gave developers a console to monitor usage and add or remove servers, so the studio did not need its own operations team.
claims.locator: Blocks 'Focus on building your game, not the back end' and 'HeroCloud gets you a license to the HeroEngine for just $99 per year'; corroborated by SRC-HE-010 paragraph on integrated billing and SRC-HE-020 block 'Game Development'
claims.context: Vendor marketing (archived) plus vendor corporate site. Describes the service model; gives no SLA, uptime or capacity figures.

claims.statement: The HeroCloud proposition promised immediate cloud provisioning with zero server or local-network setup: 'UP AND RUNNING in the cloud immediately' and 'EDIT in the same environment with the rest of your team, in real-time. No local network set-up.'
claims.locator: Homepage banner bullet list ('UP AND RUNNING in the cloud immediately', 'EDIT in the same environment ... No local network set-up')
claims.context: Archived vendor homepage (2013). Marketing claim; no provisioning time or setup-effort figure is given.

claims.statement: HeroEngine/HeroCloud servers ran on both Microsoft Windows and Linux, with official support for CentOS and a full Linux build system available to source-code licensees, allowing homogeneous or heterogeneous Windows/Linux server fleets.
claims.locator: Section 'Windows & Linux Server Support' (bullets: 'Official support for CentOS', 'Full Linux build system for source code licensees', 'Ability to run servers in a full Linux environment, full Windows environment, or a heterogeneous mix')
claims.context: Vendor server-systems page (archived). States supported server OSes; no hardware sizing or concurrency figures.

claims.statement: Idea Fabrik, the company that owned HeroEngine and HeroCloud, disappeared from the internet in 2023: its website, social media and the heroengine.com site went dead, and its contracted development team had quit The Repopulation earlier that year.
claims.locator: Opening and second paragraphs (reporting that 'the website for the Hero Engine no longer works' and that the contracted dev team quit in January 2023)
claims.context: Independent MMO trade journalism (April 2023). Describes company status at that date; it does not establish a formal corporate dissolution.

claims.statement: A secondary article states that Idea Fabrik PLC was formally dissolved in 2025 and that HeroEngine's last stable release was version 2.074 in January 2024, leaving it a legacy product with only limited support.
claims.locator: Sections 'Is HeroEngine Still Used Today?' and 'History and Ownership'
claims.context: Secondary article (updated 2026). The version number is corroborated by SRC-HE-002, but the 2025 dissolution date is not attributed to a primary registry document in the opened text, so it is marked unverified.

claims.statement: PlayM2M, a free-to-play mythological-fantasy MMORPG, entered Steam Early Access on 28 March 2025, developed and published by Laniatus LLC.
claims.locator: Steam store metadata block: Developer 'Laniatus LLC', Publisher 'Laniatus LLC', 'Early Access Release Date: 28 Mar, 2025'
claims.context: Storefront metadata. Confirms the title shipped; it says nothing about the engine, so it cannot support a HeroEngine claim.

claims.statement: The attribution of PlayM2M to HeroEngine is unconfirmed. A secondary article states PlayM2M was built on the engine, but Laniatus's own site describes an in-house engine and never names HeroEngine or HeroCloud, so PlayM2M is deliberately NOT recorded as a HeroEngine game example in this pack.
claims.locator: Sections 'We build the engine beneath the game' and 'The platform / Engine runtime' (Laniatus describes an in-house engine; no mention of HeroEngine/HeroCloud); contrast SRC-HE-004 section 'Games Made with HeroEngine'
claims.context: Gap/conflict. Missing evidence would be a first-party Laniatus or PlayM2M statement naming HeroEngine, or engine attribution in the game's own files.

claims.statement: Idea Fabrik's corporate site positions HeroCloud as a PaaS that abstracts operations for the studio - 'We manage servers, bandwidth, hosting, billing, etc.' - and its news list records the 13 January 2017 acquisition of The Repopulation.
claims.locator: Blocks 'Agile Development', 'Game Development' ('We manage servers, bandwidth, hosting, billing, etc.') and news list entry 'Friday, 13 January 2017: Idea Fabrik acquires The Repopulation'
claims.context: Vendor corporate site (largely static legacy page). Confirms vendor positioning and the Repopulation acquisition; it contains no technical or measured content.

claims.statement: No source opened in this assignment states what HeroCloud hosting or licensing terms (if any) are offered after Idea Fabrik's 2023 disappearance. The live heroengine.com page still exists but serves only a login/landing page with no pricing or service description.
claims.locator: Homepage content (login form, 'HeroCloud Login', 'Last Updated: 09.27.2024 ... Version: 3.0') - no pricing or service terms present
claims.context: Gap. Missing evidence would be a current vendor service page, an official migration notice, or a successor company's terms of service.

game_examples.fact: A Kickstarted sci-fi sandbox MMO that entered Steam early access in 2014 and was tied to HeroEngine; a HeroEngine contract dispute took the game offline for a year before Idea Fabrik acquired it in 2017.
game_examples.locator: SRC-HE-016 opening paragraphs ('The Repopulation ... hit Steam early access in 2014 ... the year it was offline entirely thanks to the HeroEngine dispute'); SRC-HE-020 news list 'Friday, 13 January 2017: Idea Fabrik acquires The Repopulation'
game_examples.non_transferable: Evidences a HeroEngine/HeroCloud-dependent live title and the operational risk of depending on the vendor. It does NOT evidence a player count, shard size or any measured performance figure.

game_examples.fact: The flagship HeroEngine title, licensed in 2008 and shipped in 2011; as a large studio it took a source-code license rather than the HeroCloud subscription.
game_examples.locator: SRC-HE-003 body paragraph (BioWare license announcement, 2008); SRC-HE-010 section 'HeroEngine Source Code' (the alternative to the $99/yr HeroCloud license)
game_examples.non_transferable: Listed only to delimit the HeroCloud evidence: SWTOR is evidence for the engine, NOT for HeroCloud. Do not cite SWTOR as proof that HeroCloud can host a large live MMO - it was a source-code licensee.

claims.statement: HeroScript (HSL) is the engine's first-class scripting language, described by the vendor as a 'robust, type-safe hybrid Object Oriented and Procedural language' that combines object-oriented and procedural features with rapid debugging, and that is used to define game behaviour, mechanics and systems.
claims.locator: Section 'HeroScript' (paragraphs 'HeroScript combines object-oriented and procedural features...' and 'HeroScript is a first-class development language, featuring a robust, type-safe hybrid Object Oriented and Procedural language')
claims.context: Vendor language description (archived). Establishes the vendor's characterisation of HSL; no grammar or type-system specification is provided.

claims.statement: The vendor claims HeroScript is 'faster than Python and more targeted at MMO development than any other language', and states its virtual machine is designed so that scripting errors are never fatal.
claims.locator: Section 'HeroScript', final paragraph ('HeroScript is faster than Python ... with a virtual machine that is bulletproof because scripting errors must never be fatal')
claims.context: Vendor marketing assertion with no benchmark attached. The comparative speed claim against Python is unverified and must not be reused as a measured figure.

claims.statement: HeroScript is authored in a built-in editor integrated into HeroBlade that provides syntax highlighting plus versioning, history, diff and merge, and HeroSense adds script assistance to that editor: automatic minor syntax correction, intelligent list boxes, and tooltips with definitions, parameters and return types.
claims.locator: Sections 'Scripting' and 'HeroSense' (bullets 'Automatic minor syntax correction', 'Tooltips with definitions, parameters, and return types'); corroborated by SRC-HE-009 section 'HeroScript' (editor 'with support for versioning, history, diff and merge')
claims.context: Vendor editor description (archived). Describes IDE features; no editor performance figures.

claims.statement: HSL is event-driven rather than main-loop driven: the official wiki documents 'Script Entry Points' explaining that the engine has no main loop, alongside a 'Commands Syntax Reference' of hardcoded HSL commands, an 'HSL for programmers' quickstart, and 'Your First HSL Script' tutorial.
claims.locator: HEWIKI Main Page, 'Scripting' section page list ('Your First HSL Script', 'HSL for programmers', 'Commands Syntax Reference', 'Script Entry Points' described as 'the engine is event-driven (no Main Loop)')
claims.context: Official wiki index (archived). Evidences the existence and topic of HSL documentation pages; the individual pages were not opened, so their detailed contents are not evidenced here.

claims.statement: HSL has server-side reach: the vendor states developers can create new processes and assign asynchronous tasks directly from HeroScript, that spatial awareness is available for general use via HeroScript, and that the HeroPath pathfinding system is fully accessible from HeroScript.
claims.locator: Intro paragraph ('You can even create new processes and assign asynchronous tasks all from HeroScript'); sections 'Spatial Awareness' ('Available for general use via HeroScript') and 'HeroPath' ('fully accessible from HeroScript')
claims.context: Vendor server-systems page (archived). Shows HSL is not client-only; no API surface or performance data is given.

claims.statement: No opened source provides an HSL language specification, grammar, standard-library listing, or any measured execution benchmark. The only quantitative performance statement found is the vendor's unbenchmarked 'faster than Python' claim.
claims.locator: Section 'HeroScript' contains no benchmark numbers; the wiki index (SRC-HE-011) lists tutorials and a command reference but no specification page was opened
claims.context: Gap. Missing evidence would be the HSL Commands Syntax Reference contents, a language spec, or an independent benchmark.

game_examples.fact: Shipped on HeroEngine, whose gameplay logic language is HSL; the studio has since stated that little of the original engine code remains and that the UI/rendering had to be rebuilt for DirectX 12.
game_examples.locator: SRC-HE-003 body paragraph (HeroEngine license, 2008); SRC-HE-015 section 'Next Steps' ('little of the original code remains')
game_examples.non_transferable: Evidences a shipped title on the engine that HSL belongs to. It does NOT evidence that shipped SWTOR gameplay code is written in HSL today, and the studio confirms the engine has been largely rebuilt.

game_examples.fact: A 2011 HeroEngine MMORPG; as a HeroEngine title its gameplay logic would be authored in HSL, though no opened source names the language for this title.
game_examples.non_transferable: Only evidences a second shipped HeroEngine title, whose scripting language is by construction HSL. No source opened confirms HSL usage on this project specifically.

claims.statement: HeroEngine partitions the world by geography into individual area servers and supports three area models - common areas, instanced areas, and hybrid approaches - letting a developer choose a heavily instanced game, a seamless world, or a mixture.
claims.locator: Intro paragraph: 'Segregate your geography into individual area servers. HeroEngine supports common areas, instanced areas, and hybrid approaches. Choose a heavily instanced style of game, or a seamless world, or some mixture in between'
claims.context: Vendor server-systems page (archived). This is the clearest opened statement of HeroEngine's instancing model; it is architectural description, not a measured result.

claims.statement: Shared and instanced area instances can be connected into one continuous seamless world: transitions between shared areas, instanced areas or both are supported, replication keeps clients up to date automatically, game logic functions transparently across server boundaries, and positions are translated automatically between servers/areas.
claims.locator: Section 'Seamless Worlds' (bullets 'Full support for seamless transitions between shared areas, instanced areas, or both', 'Game logic functions transparently when interactions cross server boundaries', 'Automatic translation of positions from other servers and world areas to match the current area')
claims.context: Vendor world-building page (archived). Describes the seamless-world capability; no player-count or boundary-crossing latency figures.

claims.statement: Instanced/streamed areas use a room system: an area can contain an unlimited number of rooms, each room can be set to render or not render adjacent rooms to save render cost, and transitional pieces allow large texture-bank swaps as a player moves between areas, producing the appearance of a seamless world.
claims.locator: Section 'Seamless World and Instances' (paragraphs on the room visualization system and transitional pieces)
claims.context: Vendor world-building page (archived). Describes the streaming/instancing mechanism; the word 'unlimited' is the vendor's own claim and is not a measured limit.

claims.statement: The official wiki defines the engine's scaling vocabulary: a 'Cluster' is multiple machines including a database plus 1..N world servers; a 'Shard/World' is a game-world instance that splits the total population; an 'Area Instance' is a Play or Edit instance of an area running in a single process (the unit of simulation); and 'Instance Slices' are area instances spun up to distribute load for a specific region of geometry.
claims.locator: Section 'Terminology' table (rows 'Cluster', 'Shard / World', 'Area Instance', 'Instance Slices')
claims.context: Official wiki (archived, 2011). Provides the authoritative definitions for the entity's 'instancing/sharding' scope; note the engine's own term is 'Area Instance', and 'Instance Slices' is its load-distribution mechanism.

claims.statement: For an illustrative budget of 10 MHz of processing per user on a 3 GHz machine, the wiki derives approximately 300 users per area server, noting the real figure is lower in practice because operations such as broadcast chat do not scale linearly.
claims.locator: Section 'Per Area Instance' ('Specific example budget: 10 MHz per user on a 3 GHz machine -> approximately 300 users per area server (less in practice ...)')
claims.context: Vendor wiki worked example (archived). It is an illustrative budget calculation published by the vendor, explicitly a simplification ('less in practice'), not a measurement of any shipped title.

claims.statement: The wiki reports that 5,000 AI-controlled characters were run inside a single area server instance on a single core of roughly three-year-old commodity hardware, with simple wandering AI and the characters placed in packets of 100 so each received awareness events for at most 99 others.
claims.locator: Section 'Per Area Instance' ('5000 AI-controlled characters were personally run in a single area server instance ... placed in packets of 100 ...')
claims.context: Vendor wiki anecdote (archived). Applies to simple AI under specific awareness-packing conditions; it is NOT a player-capacity figure and must not be generalised to players or complex AI.

claims.statement: The engine's simulation and rendering run on a single thread (as reported in the encyclopedia article citing the official forum), with a multi-threaded release planned but no published date.
claims.locator: Section 'Features' ('The simulation and rendering processes of the engine are currently run on a single-thread. However, it is planned for there to be a multi-threaded release, but the publish date has not yet been determined')
claims.context: Secondary source citing an official forum post; the forum post itself was not opened, and the statement describes the engine at an unspecified time (the article is undated for this claim). Treat the single-threaded limitation as era-dependent.

claims.statement: The engine's own documentation does not use the term 'sharding': the closest official concepts are geographic area-server segregation and organising an environment into separate public and private worlds, so 'sharding' is an external label rather than a HeroEngine term.
claims.locator: Server Systems page - the word 'sharding' does not appear; partitioning is described as 'Segregate your geography into individual area servers' and 'Organize your environment into separate worlds, both public and private' (Master Control Console section)
claims.context: Based on the full text of the opened server-systems page. It is a statement about terminology in one vendor document, not a claim that HeroEngine cannot shard; the wiki (SRC-HE-012) separately defines 'Shard / World'.

claims.statement: No opened source states a measured maximum concurrent-player count, shard population, or area count for any shipped HeroEngine title. All capacity figures found are the vendor's illustrative budgets on the wiki, not telemetry from a live game.
claims.locator: Section 'Per Production Cluster' and 'Per World / Shard' give only 'tens of thousands ... millions' style ranges; no shipped-title telemetry appears anywhere on the page
claims.context: Gap. Missing evidence would be a HeroEngine postmortem, a studio capacity talk, or an operational metric from a live HeroEngine title.

game_examples.fact: A large-scale live MMORPG that shipped on HeroEngine, which natively supports geographic area servers and instanced areas; the studio has since largely rebuilt the engine.
game_examples.locator: SRC-HE-003 body paragraph (2008 license); SRC-HE-008 intro paragraph (area-server and instanced-area support); SRC-HE-015 section 'Next Steps'
game_examples.non_transferable: Evidences that a shipped title used the engine offering these instancing features. It does NOT evidence how SWTOR partitioned its world, nor any shard size or player count.

game_examples.fact: A sandbox MMO that ran on HeroEngine/HeroCloud in Steam early access from 2014, and was taken offline for a year by a HeroEngine contract dispute.
game_examples.locator: SRC-HE-016 opening paragraphs; SRC-HE-020 news list entry 'Friday, 13 January 2017: Idea Fabrik acquires The Repopulation'
game_examples.non_transferable: Evidences a second shipped HeroEngine title and the vendor-dependency risk. It does NOT evidence instancing behaviour, shard counts or concurrency for that game.
